examples.before:
.troupe/troupe.yml:
model: opus  # main model
retries: 3
prompt: file:prompts/system.txt
agents:
  coder: file:agents/coder.yaml

results.1:
exit 0; prints:
opus # from .troupe/troupe.yml
(the file's own `# main model` comment is not shown; no files changed)

exit 0; prints:
0.2 # from .troupe/agents/coder.yaml
(gives the included file, not troupe.yml)

exit 0; prints a literal block:
| # from .troupe/prompts/system.txt
  You are helpful.
  Be brief.

exit 0; prints the plain text:
You are helpful.
Be brief.

exit 0; prints:
temperature: 0.2 # from .troupe/agents/coder.yaml
name: Coder # from .troupe/agents/coder.yaml
(the quotes around "Coder" are dropped)

context.in_practice: All six implementations on route 1 gave exactly the same results, and no command changed any file. With --sources, a single value prints on one line with a `# from <file>` comment. A value that comes from an included text file becomes a `|` block with the comment on its first line. Without --sources, you get just the raw value.
context.stakes: When you ask where a single value comes from, you need output that names the file it was read from and is still valid YAML, including values pulled in from a separate text file.
context.tradeoff: Route 1: the output for one value is valid YAML and names its source file, but text from an included file changes shape (indented block instead of plain text) when you add --sources, and the original file's comments and quotes are not kept.

plan_why: Shows what `show PATH --sources` prints when PATH is a scalar: a plain value, a value from a YAML include, and a multi-line text include (which this route prints as a literal block with the comment), with plain `show` alongside for contrast.
routes: One-scalar YAML with the comment; a text include becomes a literal block
